title: S3 Presigned URLs: Is Direct-to-S3 File Upload Secure?
content:
S3 Presigned URLs: Is Direct-to-S3 File Upload Secure? A familiar situation when building a document management application: a user selects a file, the frontend sends it to the backend, and Lambda forwards it to Amazon S3. This works, but the backend has to receive and transfer the entire file.
Can a browser upload directly to S3 without giving users AWS credentials? One common option is a presigned URL. But what permissions does the URL grant, can it be reused, and what should we consider if it is exposed?
01 | WHAT PERMISSIONS DOES A PRESIGNED URL GRANT? A presigned URL is an HTTP request to S3 signed with the credentials of an IAM principal. An application can give the URL to a client so it can perform a specific operation for a limited time, such as PUT to upload or GET to download.
The client does not need to hold AWS access keys. The request remains limited by the permissions of the principal that created the URL, along with the bucket, object key, HTTP method, and expiration that were signed. In other words, it is a way to grant temporary use of a predefined request, not a standalone user authorization system.
AWS describes presigned URLs as bearer tokens: anyone who has the URL can use it while it is valid. Treat it like a credential and protect it accordingly. [1]
02 | THE DIRECT-TO-S3 UPLOAD FLOW For a document management application, an upload flow could work as follows:
The user signs in and requests to upload a document. The backend authenticates the user, checks business permissions, and creates a unique object key, such as incoming/user-123/uuid.pdf. The backend uses its IAM role to create a presigned URL for the specific bucket, object key, HTTP method, and expiration. The backend returns the URL to the browser. The browser sends the file directly to S3 with a PUT request. After S3 receives the object, a follow-up workflow can validate the file and update the document status. In this flow, Lambda authenticates and grants temporary access, while the file contents travel directly from the browser to S3. The bucket can remain private; the presigned URL only allows the specified signed request to access the designated object during its validity period. [1][2]
03 | A URL IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY SINGLE-USE An easy-to-miss detail: a presigned URL can be used multiple times until it expires. If an object with the same key already exists, another PUT can replace that object. [1][2]
For that reason, do not let the client choose a shared key such as uploads/report.pdf. The backend should create a unique, hard-to-guess key for each upload, associate it with the user or business record, and sign only the required operation.
If you need to constrain uploads to a specific size range, consider a presigned POST with a content-length-range policy condition. Do not assume that a presigned PUT automatically meets every application-level file-size requirement. [3]
04 | URL LIFETIME ALSO DEPENDS ON THE SIGNING CREDENTIALS A presigned URL has a configured expiration, but it cannot remain valid longer than the credentials used to sign it. If the URL is signed with temporary IAM role credentials, it may stop working when that session ends, even if the configured URL expiration is later.
The AWS CLI and SDKs allow expiration settings of up to seven days under the applicable conditions. That is a maximum, not a sensible default for every use case. Choose a duration that is long enough for the operation and consider whether users may need to retry. The longer a URL lives, the longer the window for someone to use it if it is exposed. [1]
05 | CORS LETS THE BROWSER CALL S3, BUT DOES NOT AUTHENTICATE USERS When the frontend and bucket are on different origins, the browser may send a preflight request. The bucket’s CORS configuration must allow the correct origin, methods such as PUT, and the request headers the application actually sends.
However, CORS only controls how browsers allow JavaScript to call a resource on another origin. It does not authenticate users, replace IAM or bucket policies, or prevent another HTTP client from using an exposed URL. S3 permissions and policies still apply. [4]
A common error is SignatureDoesNotMatch. The upload request must match what was signed, including the HTTP method and relevant headers. For example, if Content-Type was included when the URL was created, the client must send the same value with the upload. If this error occurs, check that the URL was not changed, has not expired, uses the correct region, and that the headers match. [2]
06 | A SUCCESSFUL UPLOAD DOES NOT MEAN THE FILE IS SAFE A presigned URL transfers a file to S3, but it does not confirm that the file has the expected business format, is safe, or may later be viewed by that user.
One possible design is to upload into a prefix such as incoming/, then run validation and update the status to PENDING, READY, or REJECTED. For downloads, the backend should still re-check the user’s permissions and the document’s status before issuing an appropriate URL.
If S3 Event Notifications start processing after an upload, account for their at-least-once delivery model: notifications can be delayed, duplicated, and are not guaranteed to arrive in the order the events occurred. Consumers should tolerate retries and process duplicates safely, for example by using the object key together with a version or a stored processing identifier. Also avoid having a Lambda write objects into the same prefix that triggers it unless the design prevents recursive invocation. [5]
For data that needs transfer-integrity checks, SigV4 presigned uploads support checksum headers that let S3 compare the checksum with the received content. A checksum can detect a mismatch in the transferred data, but it does not replace content validation or malware scanning. [1][6]
07 | PRODUCTION READINESS CHECKLIST ① Does the backend authenticate the user and check permissions before issuing a URL?
② Does the backend create a unique object key scoped to the intended storage area?
③ Is the bucket still private, does the IAM role have only the required permissions, and is the URL expiration appropriate?
④ Have you considered URL exposure, repeated uploads to the same key, CORS, signed headers, and checksums?
⑤ Is the file validated after upload, and can the worker safely handle duplicate or out-of-order events?
CONCLUSION Presigned URLs let a browser upload directly to S3 without holding AWS credentials or sending the entire file through Lambda. In exchange, the URL must be treated as temporary access: whoever possesses it can make the signed request until the URL or its underlying credentials expire.
A secure flow therefore involves more than “creating a URL.” The backend must decide who can upload, which object key may be used, and how long the URL remains valid. The system must also validate files after receipt and process events in a retry-safe way.
A presigned URL grants a limited request. The application must still enforce business permissions.

title: Define the Target Architecture
content:
This is the proposed target design for the UniCloud DMS workshop. The architecture diagram must be drawn and explained by the student, then updated to match the resources that are actually deployed. Do not present this target as a deployed system before verification.
Objective Define the identity, API, metadata, file-transfer, and monitoring paths before creating AWS resources.
Proposed components Component Responsibility AWS Amplify Hosting Host the React/Vite single-page frontend and provide HTTPS delivery. Amazon Cognito User Pool Register and authenticate users; issue tokens to the frontend. Amazon API Gateway HTTP API Expose document routes and validate Cognito JWTs with a JWT authorizer. AWS Lambda Enforce per-document authorization, manage metadata, and issue short-lived S3 presigned URLs. Amazon DynamoDB Store document metadata, document shares, and per-user favorites. Use on-demand capacity for the workshop workload. Amazon S3 Store file bytes in a private bucket. Browsers transfer files directly using authorized presigned URLs. AWS IAM Give each Lambda execution role only the table, bucket-prefix, and logging actions it needs. Amazon CloudWatch Collect Lambda/API logs and metrics; add alarms after the core workflow is stable. Implementation status The AWS SAM template and Lambda source are in backend/. Stack dms-dev was deployed and updated in ap-southeast-1 with a Cognito User Pool/client, HTTP API, private S3 bucket, two Lambda functions, and three on-demand DynamoDB tables. The frontend is hosted on Amplify. The deployed routes and document workflows are verified in sections 5.7 through 5.10. SAM also created the separate managed artifact bucket aws-sam-cli-managed-default-samclisourcebucket-5wpco5qcy6qp.
The API choice is an HTTP API with a Cognito JWT authorizer. API Gateway validates the token before invoking a protected route, and the verified claims are passed to Lambda. See HTTP API JWT authorizers.
Main data flows Sign-in and API request The user signs up or signs in through the React app and the Cognito User Pool. Cognito returns tokens to the frontend. The app sends the access token as Authorization: Bearer <token> to protected API routes. API Gateway validates the JWT issuer, signature, expiry, and configured app-client audience before invoking Lambda. Lambda reads the verified Cognito sub claim from the API event. It never trusts an ownerId supplied by the browser. Upload The frontend sends file metadata to POST /documents/upload-url. Lambda validates the authenticated user, filename, allowed file type, and size limit; it creates a document ID and an S3 key derived from the verified user sub. Lambda returns a short-lived presigned PUT URL. The browser uploads the bytes directly to the private S3 bucket. The frontend calls POST /documents/{documentId}/complete. Lambda verifies that the object exists and records metadata in DynamoDB. If completion fails after the object upload, the object is treated as an orphan and can be retried or removed by a documented cleanup process. S3 presigned URLs provide time-limited access to a specific object without making the bucket public. See S3 presigned URLs.
List, view, and download The frontend requests the user’s documents or a document detail using a valid Cognito token. Lambda queries metadata using the authenticated sub and checks owner or active Viewer-share access for document-specific requests. For an authorized download, Lambda returns a short-lived presigned GET URL. The browser downloads directly from S3. Share, favorite, and Trash The owner can create or revoke a Viewer share. The recipient can list, view, and download the document while it is active. A favorite is stored as a relationship between a Cognito sub and a document, not as a client-controlled list of emails. Moving a document to Trash is a soft delete in metadata. A trashed document is hidden from normal and shared views. Restore makes the document active again; permanent deletion is a separate owner-only operation. Monitoring Lambda writes structured application logs to CloudWatch. API Gateway access logs and service metrics are used to validate requests, errors, and latency. Logs must not contain passwords, tokens, presigned URLs, or file contents.
Security boundaries to draw The browser is an untrusted client. All authorization decisions happen in Lambda using API Gateway verified claims. The S3 bucket blocks public access. Only Lambda’s execution role can access the required bucket prefix; the browser receives time-limited object access through presigned URLs. API Gateway only invokes the configured Lambda integrations. Lambda roles are scoped to the specific DynamoDB tables and S3 bucket prefix. Cognito app-client identifiers may be used in frontend configuration; AWS secret keys and other server credentials must never be shipped to the browser. S3 CORS permits only the local development origin and the final Amplify site origin, with the upload/download methods and headers actually required. Deployed architecture diagram The diagram distinguishes user traffic from the GitHub-to-Amplify deployment path. It shows Cognito-issued JWTs, the API Gateway HTTP API routes, the documents and health Lambda functions, all three DynamoDB tables, private S3 with direct browser transfers using presigned URLs, the shared Lambda execution role, and the observed CloudWatch runtime logs.
Expected result The written architecture and editable diagram describe the deployed system. Review the diagram labels against the deployment before submitting the report.
Troubleshooting A JWT authorizer authenticates the token, but Lambda still has to check document ownership or share permissions. A presigned URL is a bearer capability. Keep its expiry short and never log or store the URL in DynamoDB. Do not route file bytes through Lambda. If the browser cannot upload to S3, check the URL method, signed content type, bucket CORS, and the Lambda role.

title: FCAJ Community Day
content:
Event Report: FCAJ Community Day Event Information Date and time: 09:00–12:00, Saturday, October 31, 2026 Location: Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Attendee Program: FCAJ Community Day on Luma Speakers The event featured speakers from technology companies and the FCAJ community:
Thinh Nguyen – STYL Solutions Henry Duc Bui – CloudThinker Hung Tran – NAB Dao Luong – FCAJ Khang Duong – FCAJ Tuan Tran – FCAJ What I Heard at the Event Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories The program opened with practical lessons from building software factories at scale. The talk covered common pitfalls and approaches that have worked for teams doing this in practice. I took away that as software development grows, processes and tools should help teams work consistently instead of simply adding more steps or technology.
Education and Preparing Cloud Talent The Education session shared an educator’s perspective on preparing the next generation of cloud talent. It discussed what students should prepare before entering the industry and how universities and businesses can bridge the gap between academic learning and workplace needs. I was reminded that students need both foundational knowledge and hands-on practice through projects that apply that knowledge to concrete problems.
AWS Lambda Web Functions and Serverless Architecture The AWS Lambda Web Functions session introduced a new way to run web applications on Lambda. The presentation covered native HTTP support and concurrent request handling, with the program highlighting up to 128 concurrent requests. It also discussed reducing adapter overhead, Active CPU Billing, and live performance benchmarks against Docker deployments on EC2/ECS.
From this session, I learned to consider how an application receives requests, its concurrency needs, compute costs, and real-world performance when choosing a serverless architecture. Benchmarks can help teams make decisions based on their workloads instead of assuming that one model fits every application.
Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems In the Amazon SQS session, I heard why modern systems use asynchronous processing and how queues can decouple components. Once work is placed in a queue, the part accepting requests and the part processing them can operate more independently, helping the system absorb workload and scale separate components. The session also covered design patterns and practical implementation tips.
My main takeaway was that asynchronous processing can be useful for tasks that do not need to return a result immediately. It also requires a plan for failures, retries, and message status monitoring so that the workflow remains reliable.
My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey This session shared a three-month AWS internship experience, how AWS services were applied to a real project, and advice for students about to begin an internship. The story showed me how learning cloud services becomes more concrete when connected to a product: students need to understand requirements, choose suitable services, and observe how the system operates.
Start and Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing The final session discussed making a first open-source contribution, building a regular contribution habit, and staying motivated. I learned that newcomers can begin with small steps, such as reading contribution guidelines, writing clear bug reports, improving documentation, or choosing a suitable issue. Contributing over time can strengthen skills in reading code, collaboration, and communication in software teams.
Key Takeaways The sessions connected cloud concepts with practical software development situations. I took away three main points: architecture choices should be based on workload and measurements; asynchronous processing reduces dependencies between components but requires failure handling; and professional skills grow through project work, internships, and community contributions.
Applying the Learning to My Project My document management project currently receives requests through API Gateway and processes them with Lambda. After the SQS session, I see a possible opportunity to explore a queue for background tasks if the project later needs notifications or longer document-processing jobs. This is a future idea, not a feature that has been implemented. The Lambda Web Functions session also gave me another architecture to investigate, but compatibility and performance should be evaluated against the application’s requirements before choosing it.
Reflection I found FCAJ Community Day useful because it combined software engineering experience, cloud architecture, an internship story, and open-source participation. The sessions gave me practical perspectives to continue learning AWS and consider possible improvements to my project.

title: CloudWatch Logs, Metrics, and Alarms
content:
The dms-dev-documents and dms-dev-health Lambda log groups in ap-southeast-1 use Never expire retention. API Gateway writes access logs to a separate log group with 7-day retention.
Objective Inspect API access logs, Lambda runtime logs/metrics, and error alarms without exposing secrets.
Implementation steps Follow the steps in order. Read the action, its explanation, and the expected check before moving to the next step.
Step 1: In the AWS Console, select ap-southeast-1 → CloudWatch → In the AWS Console, select ap-southeast-1 → CloudWatch → Logs → Log groups; open /aws/lambda/<stack>-documents or /aws/lambda/<stack>-health.
Step 2: Select the log stream around the operation time and read Select the log stream around the operation time and read START, END, and REPORT; use time/function request ID to locate an invocation. Do not treat the Lambda request ID as the API Gateway request ID.
Step 3: Set suitable retention in the Retention tab so logs are Set suitable retention in the Retention tab so logs are not stored indefinitely. Lambda publishes Invocations, Errors, and Duration in CloudWatch → Metrics → AWS/Lambda (Lambda metrics guide).
Step 4: To receive an email when Lambda errors occur, open To receive an email when Lambda errors occur, open CloudWatch → Alarms → Create alarm → select AWS/Lambda / FunctionName / Errors; use Sum, a suitable period, threshold >= 1, then select or create an SNS email topic. Recipients must confirm the email subscription (SNS email alarm guide). Alarms may incur charges.
Step 5: Do not log authorization headers, full JWTs, presigned Do not log authorization headers, full JWTs, presigned URLs, file contents, or sensitive personal data.
Step 6: For an HTTP API, create a dedicated CloudWatch log group For an HTTP API, create a dedicated CloudWatch log group, for example /aws/apigateway/<stack>-access, and set its retention. In API Gateway, open the API → Monitor → Logging, select the $default stage → Select → Edit; enable Access logging, enter the log group ARN, and choose a JSON format containing $context.requestId, $context.routeKey, $context.httpMethod, and $context.status. Save the configuration. After the API receives a request, open the log group to inspect the access event. HTTP API access-log IDs and Lambda runtime request IDs are distinct and should not be treated as the same ID.
Observed log evidence The document-function stream contains Lambda runtime START, END, and REPORT records with Lambda request IDs and duration.
The $default HTTP API stage writes JSON access logs to /aws/apigateway/dms-dev-access with 7-day retention. A browser CORS preflight record for OPTIONS /{proxy+} has status 204 and includes a request ID and request time; the source IP is redacted in the screenshot. Lambda runtime logs and API Gateway access logs are recorded in separate log groups.
The dms-dev-documents-errors alarm monitors the AWS/Lambda Errors metric for dms-dev-documents, using Sum over each 5-minute period and triggering at one or more errors (1 of 1 datapoint). Its state was OK when captured; no threshold breach appears in the displayed datapoint. The alert email successfully confirmed its subscription to the dms-dev-lambda-errors SNS topic.
Expected result The screenshots confirm Lambda runtime logs, API Gateway access logs, the dms-dev-documents-errors alarm in OK state, a confirmed SNS email subscription, and an AWS Budget email alert.
Troubleshooting If no logs appear, verify the function was invoked and the role can write logs. Log storage/ingestion can incur cost; set suitable retention.

title: Prepare the Development Environment
content:
Objective Prepare a development machine, run the frontend, and confirm that the backend can start locally before configuring AWS resources.
Required tools Git for Windows to obtain the source and manage changes. Node.js 24 LTS and npm to install dependencies, run the React/Vite frontend, and match the Lambda nodejs24.x runtime major version. AWS CLI v2 for AWS authentication and operations in later deployment steps. AWS SAM CLI to validate, build, and run the Lambda/API Gateway backend locally. Docker Desktop for Windows running when using sam local start-api. This page prepares and runs the application locally. AWS credentials are not needed to open the frontend UI or call the local health endpoint. Do not use root access keys or store access keys, passwords, JWTs, or presigned URLs in source code.
Instructions A. Get the source and run the frontend Step 1: Install the required tools Install Git, Node.js/npm, AWS CLI v2, AWS SAM CLI, and Docker Desktop. Docker Desktop must be running when using SAM local.
Step 2: Clone the application repository Run the following commands to obtain the source and enter the project directory:

title: AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 - Watch Party
content:
Summary Report: “AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 - Watch Party” Event Objectives Introduce the latest developments in cloud computing and artificial intelligence. Explore how agentic AI can support software development, business processes, and enterprise transformation. Share real-world customer stories and practical approaches to data analytics, cloud migration, and modern application development. Provide opportunities for developers, students, technology professionals, and business leaders to learn directly from AWS experts and partners. Connect attendees with the local AWS community through technical sessions, workshops, demonstrations, and networking activities. The main AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 program took place in Hanoi on September 29, 2026, with keynote presentations, technical sessions, hands-on activities, customer stories, and community networking. I attended a watch party at my company office on the 26th floor of Bitexco Tower in Ho Chi Minh City and followed the Hanoi presentations via livestream.
Event Information Main event: AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 Date: September 29, 2026 Main event venue: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi My attendance location: Company watch party, 26th floor, Bitexco Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Format: Followed the Hanoi presentations via livestream at the watch party Hanoi program format: One-day, in-person event Main Areas: Agentic AI, Data & Analytics, Cloud Migration, Modern Applications Sessions: 30+ sessions Special Activities: Expo, Startup Zone, Developer Community Zone, Workshops, and 8-Bit Agents Activation Keynote Speakers The official AWS event page listed the following keynote speakers:
H.E. Hoang Minh – Deputy Minister of Science and Technology H.E. Jennifer Wicks – U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Dr. Werner Vogels – CTO, Amazon.com Eric Yeo – Country General Manager Malaysia, Vietnam, Indochina, AWS Mai Le – Director of Product Management, Katalon Dr. Jens Lottner – Chief Executive Officer, Techcombank Key Highlights Agentic AI One of the most prominent themes of the event was agentic AI.
Rather than focusing only on traditional chat-based AI, the event highlighted the idea of AI systems that can take actions, interact with tools, support workflows, and help organizations solve more complex tasks.
This theme appeared across several sessions, including:
From Demo to Deployment: Solving Agentic AI’s Toughest Challenges Building software like never before with agentic AI Migration at Scale with Agentic AI: AWS Transform and Beyond Amazon Quick Play & Build: Create Your AI Assistant, Compete, Win What I found particularly interesting was the shift in perspective from simply asking AI questions toward building systems in which AI can participate as part of an actual workflow.
Building Software with Agentic AI The session “Building software like never before with agentic AI” showed that AI is increasingly becoming part of the software development process.
For developers, this suggests a future where AI can support multiple stages of development rather than being used only for code completion.
From a student perspective, this made me think about how AI tools could assist with:
Understanding requirements Generating and explaining code Testing applications Debugging Improving development productivity The event therefore connected AI with practical software engineering rather than treating AI as an isolated technology.
Data as the Foundation for AI Another important topic was the session “Build and AI-ready data foundation.”
This highlighted an important idea: AI applications are only as useful as the data that supports them.
For organizations, preparing data for AI involves more than simply collecting a large amount of information. Data needs to be accessible, well-managed, and suitable for analytics and AI workloads.
This topic helped me understand that building an AI system is not only about choosing a powerful model. The underlying data architecture is equally important.
Cloud Migration and Modernization The event also focused on migration and modernization through the session “Migration at Scale with Agentic AI: AWS Transform and Beyond.”
This showed how AI can become part of the modernization process, especially when organizations need to deal with large existing systems and workloads.
Instead of viewing migration as simply moving applications from one environment to another, modernization requires organizations to think about:
Application architecture Scalability Operational efficiency Security Long-term maintainability This was especially relevant to me because it connected cloud technology with real business and engineering problems rather than focusing only on infrastructure.
Internal Developer Platforms and Cloud-Native Development The agenda also included “Platform Engineering at Scale: Internal Developer Platform on EKS”, presented with VPBank.
This session demonstrated another direction of modern cloud development: instead of asking every developer to manage infrastructure independently, organizations can create internal platforms that simplify development and deployment.
This helped me see how technologies such as containers, Kubernetes, and platform engineering can be combined to improve developer productivity in larger organizations.
Security and Workload Identity One of the advanced sessions was “Beyond IAM Roles: Engineering Workload Identity on AWS,” presented with Vingroup.
This topic was especially interesting from a cloud-security perspective because identity is a fundamental part of protecting cloud workloads.
It reinforced the idea that cloud security is not only about protecting networks and data, but also about carefully controlling which workloads, applications, and services are allowed to access resources.
Amazon Quick and Hands-on AI The event also provided practical activities around Amazon Quick, including:
“Amazon Quick Play & Build: Create Your AI Assistant, Compete, Win.”
AWS described this as a hands-on activity where participants could build their own AI assistant and interact with the technology directly.
The event also featured the 8-Bit Agents Activation, which was designed to let participants build and deploy AI agents through an interactive experience.
These activities were useful because they demonstrated how AI concepts can move from theory into something that users can actually build and experiment with.
Key Takeaways 1. AI Is Moving Toward Agentic Systems One of my biggest takeaways from the event was the growing importance of agentic AI.
AI is increasingly being integrated into applications and workflows instead of being used only as a question-and-answer interface.
This means developers need to think not only about models, but also about:
Tools Data Workflows Security Human oversight 2. Data Infrastructure Is Essential I also learned that AI development cannot be separated from data architecture.
A strong AI application requires data that is:
Available Reliable Well organized Secure Suitable for the intended AI workload Therefore, learning cloud databases, storage, analytics, and data pipelines is still very important even in the age of generative AI.
3. Modern Applications Require Multiple AWS Services Another important lesson was that modern applications are rarely built around a single service.
Depending on the problem, developers may combine:
Compute Databases Storage Identity APIs AI services Monitoring DevOps tools This connected strongly with what I am currently learning about serverless architecture.
4. Security Must Be Designed from the Beginning The sessions related to workload identity reinforced the importance of authorization and access control.
Instead of adding security after an application is finished, developers should think about identity and permissions during the architecture design stage.
5. Cloud Is More Than “Moving to the Cloud” Before learning about cloud architecture, it is easy to think that cloud migration simply means moving an existing application to AWS.
The event showed me that cloud migration can also be an opportunity to:
Modernize architecture Improve scalability Automate operations Introduce AI capabilities Improve developer productivity Applying What I Learned to My Project The event also gave me several ideas that I can apply to my own Serverless Document Management System project.
My current architecture uses:
Amazon Cognito for authentication AWS Amplify for frontend hosting Amazon API Gateway for REST APIs AWS Lambda for backend logic Amazon DynamoDB for document metadata Amazon S3 for document storage Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring The event helped me understand that these services should not be viewed separately.
Instead, they form a complete system in which:
User ↓ Cognito ↓ Frontend ↓ API Gateway ↓ Lambda ↓ DynamoDB / S3 ↓ CloudWatch Event Photos Attendees listening to a presentation Participants following the event on screen Another view of the audience

title: Design the Data Model and API Contract
content:
This section records the data model and API behavior observed in the deployed dms-dev stack. The example item and route catalog describe the implementation contract.
Objective Replace browser-only mock data with stable identifiers, explicit access patterns, and API routes that both frontend and Lambda can implement.
Identity and authorization rules Cognito sub is the stable internal user identifier. Email is used for sign-in and share-recipient lookup, not as the authorization key. The frontend never sends ownerSub as an authority. Lambda derives the caller identity from verified API Gateway JWT claims. Every document read, download, update, share, trash, restore, or delete checks ownership or active share permission in Lambda. A Viewer can read and download an active shared document and manage their own favorite. A Viewer cannot edit metadata, share, trash, restore, or delete it. On share creation, Lambda resolves the recipient email to a Cognito sub. Do not expose an unrestricted user-enumeration route. DynamoDB tables Use three small on-demand tables for clear access patterns. File bytes remain in S3; DynamoDB stores only metadata and relationships. Key and index design should follow application access patterns. See DynamoDB data modeling.
Table Primary key Index Purpose dms-dev-documents documentId (String) OwnerIndex: partition ownerSub, sort createdAtDocumentId Document metadata and owner listing. Sort value is ISO timestamp plus #documentId for stable ordering. dms-dev-shares recipientSub (String), documentId (String) OwnerShareIndex: partition ownerSub, sort documentIdRecipientSub Viewer relationships, Shared With Me listing, and owner share management. dms-dev-favorites userSub (String), documentId (String) DocumentFavoritesIndex: partition documentId, sort documentIdUserSub Per-user favorite queries and efficient cleanup when a document is permanently deleted. Document item { "documentId": "server-generated-id", "ownerSub": "cognito-user-sub", "fileName": "original-name.pdf", "fileType": "pdf", "fileSize": 245760, "s3Key": "users/<ownerSub>/documents/<documentId>", "category": "coursework", "tags": ["aws", "report"], "description": "Project report", "uploadStatus": "ACTIVE", "createdAt": "ISO-8601 UTC timestamp", "updatedAt": "ISO-8601 UTC timestamp", "deletedAt": null, "createdAtDocumentId": "<createdAt>#<documentId>" } The deployed OwnerIndex uses ownerSub and createdAtDocumentId as separate attributes. Lambda generates the S3 key; never concatenate an unsanitized client path into it.
Share and favorite items dms-dev-shares: recipientSub, documentId, ownerSub, permission (VIEWER), sharedAt, and an optional recipient email snapshot for display. Each user-document pair is unique. dms-dev-favorites: userSub, documentId, documentIdUserSub, and favoritedAt. A user can favorite an owned or actively shared document. The reverse index supports cleanup by document ID. Trashed documents are excluded from active owner and shared views. Restore re-enables existing shares. Revoking a share removes the relationship but does not delete the S3 object. Access patterns Operation Data access List the caller’s active documents or Trash Query dms-dev-documents.OwnerIndex by verified ownerSub; separate views by deletedAt. Read or update one document Get by documentId; compare ownerSub with the verified caller, or query dms-dev-shares for active Viewer access to read-only routes. List Shared With Me Query dms-dev-shares by recipientSub, batch-get metadata, and return only non-trashed documents. List shares created by an owner Query dms-dev-shares.OwnerShareIndex by ownerSub. List favorites Query dms-dev-favorites by userSub, batch-get documents, and include only documents still accessible to the caller. Search/filter a small personal list Initially filter authorized results by filename, category, tags, and dates. This is not full-text search. Revisit if data grows. API contract All routes below use the Cognito JWT authorizer. No unauthenticated document route is provided. sub always comes from verified authorizer claims.
Method and route Purpose Main authorization POST /documents/upload-url Validate upload and return a presigned S3 PUT URL plus documentId Authenticated caller; server creates ownerSub and s3Key POST /documents/{documentId}/complete Verify the S3 object and save metadata Requesting owner only GET /documents?view=owned&status=active|trash List owned active or trashed documents Query only caller’s ownerSub GET /documents/shared List active documents shared with caller Query only caller’s recipientSub GET /documents/{documentId} Read metadata Owner or active Viewer GET /documents/{documentId}/download-url Return a presigned S3 GET URL Owner or active Viewer PATCH /documents/{documentId} Update description, category, or tags Owner only; allow-list editable fields POST /documents/{documentId}/trash Soft-delete the document Owner only POST /documents/{documentId}/restore Restore a trashed document Owner only DELETE /documents/{documentId} Permanently delete S3 object and related metadata Owner only; separate UI confirmation POST /documents/{documentId}/shares Create Viewer share using recipient email Owner only; resolve email to Cognito sub DELETE /documents/{documentId}/shares/{recipientSub} Revoke a share Owner only GET /favorites List caller’s favorite accessible documents Query only caller’s userSub PUT /documents/{documentId}/favorite Add a favorite relationship Owner or active Viewer DELETE /documents/{documentId}/favorite Remove caller’s favorite relationship Caller’s own favorite only Use consistent error responses: 400 invalid input, 401 missing or invalid token, 403 authenticated but not authorized, 404 missing document or recipient, 409 duplicate or invalid state transition, and 5xx unexpected server error. Do not reveal whether another user’s private document exists when rejecting an unauthorized request.
Upload and deletion consistency Upload has two steps because S3 and DynamoDB do not share a transaction. complete must be idempotent for the document ID and verify the object before writing ACTIVE metadata. Permanent delete spans S3 and DynamoDB. Mark the document DELETING, remove the S3 object, then remove metadata and related shares/favorites. Make this retryable; failures must not leave the document downloadable. Soft delete retains the S3 object and metadata for restore. Cleanup instructions must distinguish Trash from permanent deletion. Deployed implementation and verification The deployed table names and key/index schemas are confirmed in sections 5.4.1 and 5.4.2. API Gateway uses a JWT-protected ANY /{proxy+} route to invoke dms-dev-documents; GET /health is public, and OPTIONS /{proxy+} handles CORS preflight. Authenticated listing returned HTTP 200, while an unshared cross-account detail request returned HTTP 404 (section 5.7.2). Upload, download, metadata, Favorites, Trash/restore, and sharing were exercised through the application (sections 5.8.2 and 5.10).
The CloudFormation change set was reviewed before deployment and the stack was deployed successfully. A separate change-set screenshot and student-authored data-model diagram were not retained.
Expected result and verification status The deployed table/index design and observed access behavior are recorded above. Authenticated listing returned HTTP 200; an unshared cross-account detail request returned 404.
Implementation progress The SAM template defines the three deployed tables, and Lambda implements authenticated presigned S3 upload/download, owner/Viewer checks, soft delete, sharing, and Favorites. sam validate --lint and sam build succeeded. The reviewed CloudFormation change set completed successfully; the stack was deployed in ap-southeast-1. Deployed outputs and current resource evidence are recorded in section 5.9.2. The public /health endpoint returned {"status":"ok","service":"dms-api"}. Authenticated document workflows were subsequently verified in sections 5.7 through 5.10.
The change set was reviewed before deployment; a separate screenshot of the change-set review screen was not retained.
The current CloudFormation resource view lists 13 resources in the dms-dev stack. The visible entries include the Cognito user pool and client, API Gateway API and stage, and the S3 documents bucket. Physical resource IDs are redacted in the report copy.
Troubleshooting If a normal list view needs a table scan, revisit the key and index design. If the frontend sends an email as ownerSub, stop and derive identity from authorizer claims. If full-text search is required, document it as a future extension; DynamoDB metadata queries do not search file contents.

title: Configure CORS and Presigned URL Transfers
content:
The deployed bucket CORS configuration is captured below. The frontend’s presigned upload and download flows are recorded in section 5.8.2.
Objective Allow only the frontend origins needed for direct browser upload/download while keeping S3 private.
Implementation steps Follow the steps in order. Read the action, its explanation, and the expected check before moving to the next step.
Step 1: Add exact origins to the SAM stack’s Add exact origins to the SAM stack’s AllowedFrontendOrigins: local Vite and https://<amplify-domain>. Update the stack after the Amplify domain exists; the template applies the list to the HTTP API and bucket CORS.
Step 2: In S3 Console → bucket → Permissions → CORS, compare In S3 Console → bucket → Permissions → CORS, compare GET/HEAD/PUT and the required signing/content-type headers. Do not use * for the production origin.
Step 3: Upload flow: the frontend sends file details to Lambda Upload flow: the frontend sends file details to Lambda; Lambda verifies the Cognito caller, creates the key server-side, and returns a short-lived PUT presigned URL. The browser PUTs directly to S3 using the signed Content-Type, then calls the complete API; Lambda uses HeadObject before writing DynamoDB metadata.
Step 4: Download flow: the API verifies owner or active-share Download flow: the API verifies owner or active-share access, then returns a short-lived GET presigned URL. Never log or share the URL.
Evidence The S3 CORS configuration allows GET, HEAD, and PUT, with the required authorization, content-type, and signing headers. Its deployed AllowedFrontendOrigins parameter, including the Amplify origin, is shown in section 5.9.2. Upload and download results are documented in section 5.8.2.
Expected result The browser can transfer a test file through presigned URLs without making the bucket public.
Troubleshooting Check origin, method, headers, URL expiration, and signed content type for failures. CORS is not authorization; the backend must still verify permissions.

title: Delete Workshop Resources and Review Costs
content:
This page both explains the cleanup procedure and records the project’s actual AWS cleanup on November 19, 2026. The screenshots show the actions performed and the AWS console states observed afterwards.
Objective Safely remove resources created for this lab in dependency-aware order.
Cleanup scope The procedure below uses resource names from the workshop environment. For another environment, confirm the AWS account, Region, and resource names first. Deleting a CloudFormation stack applies only to resources managed by that stack. Amplify, CloudWatch alarms/log groups, SNS, IAM, the AWS Budget, and SAM artifacts are handled separately. Screenshots on this page come from the project’s cleanup and document the corresponding actions and results.
An initial billing review was recorded on November 18, 2026: Cost Explorer for November 1–18 displayed -$0.00 and no visible cost bars; the November Bills page displayed USD 0.00 with status Pending. This is a provisional snapshot, not a finalized invoice. The USD 10 budget is an alert, not a spending cap.
Project resources The dms-dev stack uses logical IDs such as DmsUserPool, DmsUserPoolClient, DocumentsApi, DocumentsFunction, HealthFunction, DynamoDB tables, and DocumentsBucket. The inventory screenshots record this stack’s resources before cleanup.
Resource cleanup procedure Follow the steps in order. Read the action, its explanation, and the expected check before moving to the next step.
Step 1: Begin cleanup only after saving the demo Perform cleanup only after recording the demo and when the application no longer needs to run. Save source code, reports, and any required data locally. Deleting the stack stops the backend and may permanently remove application data.
Step 2: Select the correct stack in CloudFormation Open CloudFormation → Stacks, confirm the AWS account and ap-southeast-1 Region, select dms-dev, and choose Delete. Check the stack name and deletion impact in the confirmation dialog before proceeding.
Step 3: Empty the document bucket if deletion fails If Events reports DELETE_FAILED because of DocumentsBucket, open the bucket listed in the stack’s Resources tab. From the bucket page, choose Empty to remove all contents. For a versioned bucket, remove all object versions and delete markers too. Do not confuse the document bucket with the SAM artifact bucket.
Step 4: Retry deletion and check for retained resources Wait for S3 to finish and verify no objects remain. Return to CloudFormation and choose Retry delete for dms-dev. If the bucket is empty, do not select it for retention. Use Force delete this entire stack only to finish a stack in DELETE_FAILED; AWS may retain resources that still cannot be deleted, so inspect for leftovers afterwards.
Step 5: Confirm the application stack was deleted Wait for CloudFormation to refresh and confirm dms-dev no longer appears among active stacks. Check Events or deleted stacks if the final state needs confirmation.
Step 6: Open the Amplify app To remove the separately hosted frontend, open AWS Amplify → All apps and select the serverless-document-management app.
Step 7: Delete the Amplify app Open App settings → General settings, verify the app name, and choose Delete app. In the confirmation dialog, enter delete and confirm. This action cannot be undone.
Step 8: Confirm Amplify deletion completed Wait for the success notice. AWS may report that backend resources associated with branches have been queued for deletion; verify that the app no longer appears in the Amplify app list.
Step 9: Delete the workshop CloudWatch alarm To delete the separately created alarm, open CloudWatch → Alarms, select dms-dev-documents-errors, then choose Actions → Delete and confirm.
Step 10: Delete the workshop SNS topic To delete the SNS topic created for alarm notifications, open Amazon SNS → Topics, select dms-dev-lambda-errors, and choose Delete. In the confirmation dialog, enter delete me and confirm. The topic cannot be recovered, and its subscriptions are deleted with it.
Step 11: Delete the application log groups Remove the application log groups created separately from the stack: open CloudWatch → Logs → Log Management → Log groups, find and select /aws/apigateway/dms-dev-access, /aws/lambda/dms-dev-documents, and /aws/lambda/dms-dev-health. Choose Actions → Delete log group(s), review the selected names, and confirm. Do not select log groups unrelated to the application, such as dc-common-lambda-auto-start and dc-common-lambda-auto-stop in the example screenshots.
The screenshot illustrates the console selections; compare the log group names in your own account before confirming.
Step 12: Delete the workshop IAM role After confirming that the workshop’s Lambda functions have been deleted, open IAM → Roles, find and select the dms-lambda-execution role, then choose Delete. Verify the role name in the confirmation dialog before proceeding. IAM roles are account-level resources; do not delete service roles or other roles.
Step 13: Identify and delete the SAM artifact bucket To remove the SAM artifact bucket, match the Physical ID aws-sam-cli-managed-default-samclisourcebucket-... to the SamCliSourceBucket resource in the aws-sam-cli-managed-default stack. After emptying the bucket, open Amazon S3 → Buckets, select this exact bucket, choose Delete, enter its exact name, and confirm. The suffix varies by account, so always match the actual Physical ID.
Step 14: Delete the SAM artifact stack Return to CloudFormation → Stacks, select aws-sam-cli-managed-default, and choose Delete stack. Enter the exact stack name in the confirmation dialog and choose Delete stack again.
Wait for CloudFormation to finish and check Events or the stack status. When the status is DELETE_COMPLETE, stack deletion has finished. If an error occurs, review Events to identify the remaining resource before retrying.
Step 15: Delete the workshop budget To delete the budget created for the workshop, open Billing and Cost Management → Budgets, select My Monthly Cost Budget with an amount of $10.00, then choose Actions → Delete and confirm. Do not select My-200$-budget in the example unless you have verified that it belongs to this workshop. A budget sends alerts; it does not cap spending.
Step 16: Review AWS for remaining resources Review S3 buckets, CloudFormation stacks, CloudWatch log groups/alarms, SNS topics, Amplify apps, and Billing/Cost Explorer after cleanup. Cost data can be delayed; a Bills page for an open month is not a final invoice.
Troubleshooting If the stack reports DELETE_FAILED because a bucket is not empty, empty the correct document bucket, including object versions and delete markers. If force delete is used, some resources can be retained. Look for DELETE_SKIPPED in the deleted stack resources or inspect the relevant service, then remove leftovers manually when safe. Deleting a Cognito User Pool can permanently remove test accounts. Verify it is the workshop pool.

title: Implement Document Metadata Handlers
content:
The deployed handler behavior is documented from the Lambda implementation and existing API/browser evidence. No separate Lambda test-event screenshot was captured.
Objective Implement create/list/detail/update operations using the authenticated caller and the approved data model.
Implementation steps Follow the steps in order. Read the action, its explanation, and the expected check before moving to the next step.
Step 1: Open backend/src/index.mjs and use the API Gateway Open backend/src/index.mjs and use the API Gateway dispatcher to route by method/path; read the caller sub from authorizer-verified JWT claims. Never accept an owner ID from the frontend body.
Step 2: Query the owner’s list with OwnerIndex and fetch details Query the owner’s list with OwnerIndex and fetch details by documentId; check ownership or an active share record before returning data.
Step 3: Verify the uploaded S3 object before saving metadata The upload-completion API verifies the S3 object with HeadObject, then writes its metadata item to the Documents table. Keep metadata and bytes separate: DynamoDB stores file details, while S3 stores file contents.
Step 4: Limit PATCH updates to approved metadata fields PATCH metadata accepts only description, category, and tags; validate types/limits and allow only the owner to update an active file. Return consistent DTO/error JSON with HTTP status.
Step 5: After code changes, run sam validate –lint and sam build After code changes, run sam validate --lint and sam build from backend/, then deploy using section 5.1.3 after reviewing the change set.
Example: read identity from JWT claims This excerpt is from backend/src/index.mjs; Lambda uses only the sub verified by the API Gateway JWT authorizer:
const identity = (event) => { const claims = event.requestContext?.authorizer?.jwt?.claims; if (!claims?.sub) throw new HttpError(401, "Authentication is required"); return { sub: claims.sub, email: claims.email?.toLowerCase() ?? claims.username ?? claims.sub }; }; Verification evidence The signed-in document-list API returned HTTP 200, and the cross-account request for an unshared document returned HTTP 404; see section 5.7.2. The saved category and description are visible on the document detail page, and document records are shown in DynamoDB; see sections 5.8.2 and 5.4.1. These existing screenshots are reused instead of duplicating them here. A separate Lambda console test-event invocation was not captured.
Expected result Metadata handlers operate on the correct user-scoped records.
Troubleshooting Check case-sensitive key names, index configuration, and the sub from the token. Avoid full-table scans for regular My Documents queries.

title: Replace Mock Services and Verify Features
content:
Frontend services target the deployed AWS API. The dms-dev stack update completed successfully. Cognito sign-up/sign-in, upload/download, Favorites, Trash/restore, metadata changes, and document sharing between two Cognito accounts were exercised. Additional test limits are recorded in section 5.10.
Objective Move document reads/writes to the backend and test upload/download and all existing features.
Feature verification walkthrough The application repository already contains the frontend/API integration. If you are using this source version, you do not need to rewrite the service layer. Complete section 5.8.1 first, then follow the actions below. The screenshots at the end of this page show results from the earlier verification run.
Step 1: Sign in and upload a test file Sign in with a confirmed Cognito account. In Documents, upload a supported sample file smaller than 20 MiB. Wait for the upload to finish. The expected result is that the file appears in the list with Active status.
The app performs this flow: the frontend requests a presigned URL from the API, the browser PUTs the file directly to S3, and the frontend calls the completion API. title: Proposal
content:
Serverless Document Management System A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Secure Document Storage and Management 1. Executive Summary The Serverless Document Management System (DMS) is a web application for storing, finding, and managing documents. Its frontend is built with React/Vite, while AWS managed and serverless services provide authentication, APIs, business logic, metadata storage, and file storage. Implemented features include sign-in, uploads and downloads, document metadata updates, favorites, trash/restore, and document sharing. The architecture and test results in this report describe the previously verified deployment. The project’s AWS resources were cleaned up on November 19, 2026, so there is no active production environment now.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Documents are often scattered across personal computers, messaging apps, and email, which makes them hard to find and easy to lose. There is no single place to store them, no consistent control over who can view or change a file, and no clear record of who owns which document. Traditional solutions require running and maintaining a dedicated server, while commercial document platforms are costly and more complex than a small team needs.
The Solution Amazon Cognito authenticates users and issues JWTs. The React/Vite frontend calls business APIs through an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API. A JWT authorizer validates tokens before API Gateway forwards document routes to Lambda. Lambda reads the authenticated Cognito sub claim and checks ownership or sharing permissions before processing each document. Metadata is stored in three separate DynamoDB tables for documents, shares, and favorites. For file operations, Lambda creates presigned URLs that expire after five minutes; the browser transfers file bytes directly to private S3 instead of sending them through API Gateway or Lambda. GET /health is a public health-check route, and OPTIONS /{proxy+} handles CORS preflight without JWT authorization. Both Lambda functions share an IAM execution role scoped to the runtime access required for logs, DynamoDB, and S3. CloudWatch collects Lambda logs. In the previous deployment, GitHub main was connected to Amplify for frontend build and hosting.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution gives users a single, secure place to manage documents, reduces the time spent searching for files, and provides a reusable serverless foundation for future extensions such as full-text search, document versioning, or AI-based document analysis. It also serves as a hands-on study resource for core AWS serverless services. Every service is pay-per-use and there is no hardware or licence to buy. Under the assumptions in Section 6, the AWS Pricing Calculator estimates a pre-discount cost of about $1.19 USD per month, or $14.24 USD for 12 months if usage remains constant. This is a planning estimate, not a bill; applicable free-tier allowances, discounts, taxes, and actual traffic can change the amount charged. With no upfront investment, the return comes from time saved, better document security, and automatic scaling if usage grows.
3. Solution Architecture The diagram below describes the UniCloud DMS architecture that was verified during its deployment in the ap-southeast-1 Region. AWS Amplify hosted the React/Vite frontend. Amazon Cognito handled sign-up/sign-in and issued JWTs; API Gateway HTTP API authenticated document routes and invoked Lambda. Lambda checked access, operated on three DynamoDB tables, and generated presigned URLs. The browser transferred file bytes directly to a private S3 bucket. Both Lambda functions shared an execution role, and CloudWatch received Lambda runtime logs.
Status: This diagram represents the previous deployment. The project’s AWS resources were cleaned up on November 19, 2026; the old API endpoint and frontend hosting are no longer active.
Request flow
The user accesses the AWS Amplify frontend over HTTPS. The frontend sends the user to Cognito for sign-up or sign-in; Cognito returns tokens to the frontend. The frontend calls the API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT. The JWT authorizer validates tokens for document routes. ANY /{proxy+} sends authenticated business routes to the dms-dev-documents Lambda. Public GET /health invokes dms-dev-health; OPTIONS /{proxy+} handles unauthenticated CORS preflight. Lambda reads the authenticated Cognito sub, checks access, and reads/writes metadata in the documents, shares, and favorites DynamoDB tables. For uploads and downloads, Lambda creates a presigned PUT/GET URL with a five-minute expiry and returns it to the frontend. The browser uses that URL to transfer file bytes directly to or from the private S3 bucket. The bucket blocks public access and uses SSE-S3 encryption. Lambda sends runtime logs to Amazon CloudWatch. The previous frontend deployment path was Developer → GitHub main → AWS Amplify Hosting. AWS Services Used AWS Amplify Hosting: Hosted the React/Vite SPA and automatically built/deployed from GitHub main during the previous deployment. Amazon Cognito User Pool: Managed user sign-up/sign-in and issued tokens to the frontend. Amazon API Gateway HTTP API: Received API requests and used a JWT authorizer to protect document routes. GET /health and CORS preflight are unauthenticated exceptions. AWS Lambda: dms-dev-documents handled document APIs, authorization, metadata, and presigned URLs; dms-dev-health handled health checks. Both functions shared a Lambda execution role. Amazon DynamoDB: Three on-demand tables, dms-dev-documents, dms-dev-shares, and dms-dev-favorites, stored document metadata and sharing/favorite relationships. Amazon S3: Stored document bytes in a private bucket with Block Public Access and SSE-S3 encryption. The browser transferred files directly with presigned URLs. Amazon CloudWatch Logs: Collected Lambda runtime logs. AWS IAM: Provided the shared execution role for both Lambda functions with runtime permissions scoped to the project. AWS SAM/CloudFormation: Described and deployed the backend during the previous deployment. Component Design Frontend: React/Vite app that uses Cognito for authentication and API Gateway for document operations. Authentication and authorization: API Gateway validates JWTs. Lambda uses the Cognito sub claim to identify the owner and checks recipient sharing rights in the backend. Document access does not rely on Cognito User Groups. API layer: HTTP API uses ANY /{proxy+} for the documents Lambda, public GET /health for the health Lambda, and unauthenticated OPTIONS for CORS. Business logic: Lambda handles upload/completion, lists/details, metadata updates, download URLs, favorites, trash/restore, sharing/revocation, and permanent deletion. Metadata: Three separate on-demand DynamoDB tables hold documents, shares, and favorites. Files: A private S3 bucket stores file contents. Five-minute presigned URLs let the browser transfer files without routing bytes through Lambda. Monitoring: CloudWatch Logs receives Lambda runtime logs. The diagram does not claim API Gateway access logging or alarms. Frontend CI/CD: GitHub main previously triggered Amplify build/deploy. This describes the cleaned-up environment’s former workflow, not currently active hosting. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases The project has four phases:
Research and Design: Study the AWS serverless services involved and draw the architecture (Weeks 1-2). Calculate Cost and Check Feasibility: Use the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and confirm the design fits the requirements (Week 3). Refine Architecture: Adjust the design for security, cost, and usability, for example the DynamoDB data model and IAM policies (Weeks 4-5). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Build the backend and frontend, test all document operations, and deploy to production (Weeks 6-12). Technical Requirements and Implemented Configuration
Frontend: React/Vite SPA; AWS Amplify Hosting was used during the previous deployment and connected to GitHub main. Authentication: Cognito User Pool issues JWTs; API Gateway HTTP API uses a JWT authorizer for document routes. API routing: API Gateway configures ANY /{proxy+} for the documents Lambda, public GET /health for the health Lambda, and unauthenticated OPTIONS /{proxy+} for CORS. Document operations include POST /documents/upload-url, POST /documents/{id}/complete, GET /documents, GET /documents/shared, GET /documents/{id}, PATCH /documents/{id}, GET /documents/{id}/download-url, favorite/trash/restore/shares routes, and DELETE /documents/{id}. Authorization: Lambda reads the authenticated user’s Cognito sub claim and checks owner or recipient-sharing permissions. Ownership is not accepted from the request body. Data: Three on-demand DynamoDB tables, documents, shares, and favorites; the project does not store all data in a single table. Storage: Private S3 bucket with Block Public Access and SSE-S3 encryption; uploads are limited to 20 MiB and presigned URLs expire after five minutes. IAM: Both Lambda functions use a shared execution role with permissions scoped to backend runtime needs. Monitoring: Lambda runtime logs are sent to CloudWatch Logs. Describe API Gateway access logs or alarms only when backed by corresponding configuration and evidence. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Weeks 1-2: Research AWS serverless services and design the architecture. Week 3: Estimate cost with the AWS Pricing Calculator and check feasibility. Weeks 4-5: Refine the architecture (data model, security, cost). Weeks 6-10: Implement authentication, API, Lambda functions, DynamoDB, S3, and the frontend; test each feature. Weeks 11-12: Deploy, set up monitoring, finalize documentation, and present the final demo. 6. Budget Estimation The estimate was exported from the AWS Pricing Calculator on November 18, 2026 for the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. It is a monthly, before-discounts estimate and covers the services below. The annual figure is the monthly estimate multiplied by 12; it assumes the same usage every month.
Infrastructure Costs AWS service Monthly estimate (USD) AWS Lambda $0.0062 Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) $0.0125 Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) $0.0020 Amazon S3 Standard $0.1257 Amazon Cognito (Essentials, 10 MAU) $0.0550 AWS Amplify Hosting $0.3500 Amazon CloudWatch $0.0352 AWS data transfer $0.6000 Estimated total $1.1866 (~$1.19) Estimated annual total: $14.24 USD (monthly estimate × 12).
Hardware: $0; the solution uses managed AWS services.
Monthly usage assumptions: 10,000 API Gateway HTTP API requests; 10,000 Lambda requests and 250 Lambda GB-seconds; 4,000 DynamoDB eventually consistent read request units, 2,000 standard write request units, 1 KB average item size, and 0.1 GB table storage; 5 GB of S3 Standard storage, 100 write/list requests, and 500 read requests; 10 Cognito monthly active users; 20 Amplify build minutes, 1 GB served, and 0.002 GB stored; 0.05 GB of CloudWatch standard logs ingested with one month of log retention; and 5 GB of internet data transfer out. Other optional usage shown in the calculator was excluded. These are planning assumptions, not measured production usage.
The estimate is before discounts and does not determine the final bill. Free-tier eligibility and allowances, account-specific discounts, taxes, and usage outside these assumptions may change actual charges. The estimate assumes one month of CloudWatch log retention; the deployed log groups should be configured to match this assumption if the estimated storage cost is to represent the live setup. Review usage and the AWS bill after deployment, and set AWS Budgets alerts before increasing traffic or stored data.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Unauthorized Access: High impact, low probability. Accidental Deletion or Data Loss: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Misconfiguration (CORS, IAM, API Gateway): Medium impact, medium probability. Service Limits and Lambda Cold Starts: Low impact, medium probability. Mitigation Strategies Access: Cognito authentication, Cognito authorizer, private S3 bucket, least-privilege IAM, and short-lived pre-signed URLs. Data loss: If object recovery is required, enable and test S3 Versioning before operation; the current template does not configure Versioning. Restrict delete permissions to reduce accidental deletion. Cost: AWS Budgets alerts and CloudWatch alarms; keep resources on pay-per-use. Misconfiguration: Test each integration step by step and review IAM and CORS settings before release. Performance: Use pre-signed URLs to keep large files out of API Gateway and Lambda payload limits, and keep functions small. Contingency Plans Roll back the frontend to a previous build in AWS Amplify if a deployment fails. Use an infrastructure-as-code template (such as AWS SAM or CloudFormation) to redeploy or remove the backend stack quickly. Restore documents from previous S3 object versions if files are deleted or overwritten by mistake. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: A centralized, secure platform replaces scattered document storage, with authenticated access, searchable metadata, and direct, efficient file transfer.
The serverless design scales automatically without server maintenance.
Long-term Value A reusable serverless foundation that can be extended with full-text search, document versioning, sharing, notifications, or AI-based analysis.
A practical reference project for building secure, low-cost applications on AWS.

title: AWS SAM Backend Deployment Runbook
content:
Objective Deploy the UniCloud DMS backend through a repeatable workflow. AWS SAM transforms backend/template.yaml into a CloudFormation stack. The stack creates Cognito, an HTTP API, Lambda, DynamoDB, and S3 resources. Use your own AWS account, IAM role, stack name, and Region.
1. Prepare the account and CLI profile Step 1: Confirm AWS deployment access and select an account Sign in with the lab account or role provided by your organization, then choose one Region for the workshop. The sample uses ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). The deployment identity needs access to CloudFormation, Lambda, Cognito, API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, and CloudWatch, plus iam:PassRole limited to this workshop’s Lambda execution role. SAM also needs permission to create/use its separate artifact bucket.
If you do not have these permissions, ask the administrator for a lab role or permission set before continuing. Do not use root keys or grant AdministratorAccess just to bypass an error.
Step 2: Review expected costs and create an alert Open Billing and Cost Management, review pricing for the services used, and create an AWS Budget with suitable actual/forecast alerts. A budget sends notifications; it does not stop resources or cap spending.
Step 3: Configure and verify the AWS CLI profile Install AWS CLI v2 first. If your organization uses IAM Identity Center, open PowerShell and run these commands in order:
aws configure sso --profile unicloud-lab aws sso login --profile unicloud-lab aws sts get-caller-identity --profile unicloud-lab When prompted, enter the SSO start URL and SSO Region provided by your administrator, then select the lab account and permission set. If the lab does not use SSO, use an approved IAM profile. The last command must return the intended account ID; stop if it reports a different account. Do not share access keys or copy credentials into the repository.
2. Create the Lambda execution role The SAM template receives an existing role ARN through LambdaExecutionRoleArn, so create this role before deployment.
Step 1: Create a role trusted by Lambda In the AWS Console, open IAM → Roles → Create role. Select AWS service as the trusted entity, then choose the Lambda use case. This creates the trust relationship that lets Lambda assume the role. If your administrator already provided a dedicated workshop role, use it and skip role creation.
Step 2: Allow the function to write CloudWatch Logs Find and attach the AWS-managed policy AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole. It allows the function to write logs; table, bucket, and User Pool access is added separately after deployment.
Step 3: Name the role and copy its ARN Give the role a lab-specific name such as unicloud-dms-lambda-dev, create it, and open its details to copy the ARN. Keep the ARN for the deployment command. Do not attach AdministratorAccess.
3. Validate and deploy the CloudFormation stack Step 1: Validate and build the backend Open PowerShell in the backend directory of the serverless-document-management application repository. Run these commands. The first validates the SAM template; the second builds the Lambda package before upload:
sam validate --lint sam build Step 2: Enter your account ID and role in the deploy command Replace <ACCOUNT_ID> with the ID verified by AWS CLI and <ROLE_NAME> with the Lambda role name you created. You may change unicloud-dms-workshop to a lab-specific stack name, but keep it consistent in later steps. --resolve-s3 lets SAM manage an artifact bucket for the deployment package; this is not the document storage bucket. The origins below allow local development. Add the Amplify domain in section 5 after it is available.
sam deploy ` --stack-name unicloud-dms-workshop ` --region ap-southeast-1 ` --profile unicloud-lab ` --resolve-s3 ` --confirm-changeset ` --parameter-overrides "ParameterKey=LambdaExecutionRoleArn,ParameterValue=arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/<ROLE_NAME> ParameterKey=AllowedFrontendOrigins,ParameterValue=http://localhost:5173,http://127.0.0.1:5173" Step 3: Review the change set and wait for completion Review the change set shown by SAM/CloudFormation. Check the account, stack name, Region, role ARN, and resources to be created. Confirm only if they match your lab. Then open CloudFormation → Stacks, select the stack, and wait for CREATE_COMPLETE. If it reaches CREATE_FAILED or ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, open Events, read the first failed resource, and resolve the error before retrying.
Step 4: Save Outputs for the next sections In the stack details, open Outputs. Save ApiBaseUrl, UserPoolId, UserPoolClientId, DocumentsTableName, SharesTableName, FavoritesTableName, and DocumentsBucketName in private notes. These values belong to your new stack; do not copy IDs/URLs from evidence screenshots. Never store tokens, passwords, or credentials there.
The stack creates a Cognito User Pool and public app client, an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, two Lambda functions, three on-demand DynamoDB tables, a private SSE-S3 encrypted bucket, and related permissions/stage resources. The SAM artifact bucket is separate from the application’s document bucket.
4. Complete the Lambda runtime permissions After CloudFormation creates the stack, the role can write logs but cannot yet access application data. Complete the runtime policy so Lambda can access only the stack’s tables, objects, and User Pool. Do this after deployment because CloudFormation generates the bucket and User Pool IDs.
Step 1: Fill in the stack values in the sample policy Open backend/iam/lambda-runtime-policy.template.json in the application repository. Replace each placeholder:
<REGION>: the selected Region, such as ap-southeast-1. <ACCOUNT_ID>: the account ID returned by aws sts get-caller-identity. <STACK_NAME>: the name passed to --stack-name. <BUCKET_NAME>: the DocumentsBucketName Output. <USER_POOL_ID>: the UserPoolId Output. The table names follow <STACK_NAME>-documents, <STACK_NAME>-shares, and <STACK_NAME>-favorites. Confirm them in Outputs/Resources rather than guessing. Save the completed policy as a separate file and leave .template.json unchanged.
Step 2: Check the policy scope before attaching it Open the completed policy and confirm there are no remaining <...> placeholders and the JSON is valid. It should allow only the required actions on the three application tables/indexes, the bucket’s users/*/documents/* prefix, and this User Pool. Do not change a Resource to *.
Step 3: Attach the policy to the Lambda execution role In the AWS Console, open IAM → Roles → your workshop Lambda role → Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON. Paste the completed policy, choose Next, name it DmsDocumentRuntimeAccess, and create it. Return to the role and confirm that both AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and DmsDocumentRuntimeAccess appear in its permissions.
If an administrator has already attached this policy to a supplied role, inspect it and do not create a duplicate. Lambda now has the runtime permissions needed to handle document requests.
5. Connect the frontend and hosting Step 1: Create the local frontend configuration In the application repository root, copy .env.example to .env.local. Fill in the variables from CloudFormation Outputs; do not leave any replace-with-... values:
Variable Value to use VITE_AWS_REGION The stack Region VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID UserPoolId Output VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_CLIENT_ID UserPoolClientId Output VITE_API_BASE_URL ApiBaseUrl Output VITE_S3_BUCKET_NAME DocumentsBucketName Output VITE_* values are bundled into the browser, so use only public IDs/URLs. Never put AWS secret keys in them. Do not commit .env.local.
Step 2: Install packages and run the frontend locally From the application repository root, run npm ci, npm run build, and npm run dev in that order. Open the address printed by Vite, usually http://localhost:5173. Stop and restart Vite after changing .env.local. If sign-in or API calls fail, check the Output values before proceeding.
Step 3: Connect the application repository to Amplify In the AWS Console, open AWS Amplify → Create new app → Host web app, connect GitHub, then choose the serverless-document-management application repository and main branch. Confirm the build command is npm ci && npm run build and the output directory is dist. Add the five VITE_* variables from step 1 using Outputs from the same stack. Do not select the aws report repository.
Step 4: Add the Amplify domain to CORS After Amplify provides an HTTPS domain, copy the full origin containing only the scheme and hostname, for example https://main.xxxxx.amplifyapp.com. Redeploy the SAM stack with this exact origin in AllowedFrontendOrigins, retaining local origins if still needed. Do not include a trailing slash. API Gateway and S3 CORS must allow the same origin; CORS does not replace authentication or authorization.
6. Review resources and costs In CloudFormation, use the Resources tab to identify which stack owns each resource. Open the two Lambda log groups in Amazon CloudWatch when operational logs are needed. Monitor Billing and Cost Management/Budgets; Bills and Cost Explorer data may be delayed, and estimates are not final invoices.
7. Cleanup procedure When the project owner decides to end the lab, first confirm the account, Region, and stack name, then save any required information. Delete the application stack through CloudFormation to remove resources managed by that stack. If the S3 bucket contains objects, empty it first; check the SAM artifact bucket and Amplify Hosting separately because they may be outside the application stack. Review independent resources such as the IAM role and budget alert, and remove only lab-specific resources. Recheck charges after billing data has had time to update. These instructions do not mean that resources serving the current application have been deleted.
